version.changelog: Initial release: context estimation, rate limit recovery, checkpoint rollback, token budget

vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: agent-ops
Version: 1.0.0

The skill bundle provides operational tools for monitoring and recovering AI agent sessions, including a script for token usage estimation (scripts/context-usage.sh). While the intent appears to be session maintenance, the documentation (specifically references/04-rate-limit.md and references/19-checkpoint-rollback.md) describes high-risk patterns for automated terminal interaction using 'tmux send-keys' and 'git stash' operations. These capabilities represent a significant attack surface for unintended command execution or filesystem state corruption if the automated detection logic misidentifies the session state, fitting the criteria for suspicious behavior despite the lack of explicit malicious intent.

llm.summary: The skill's files, scripts, and runtime instructions are coherent with its stated purpose (agent session monitoring, rate-limit recovery, stale-session scavenging, checkpoint/rollback, token budgeting, and model-fallback); nothing requested is disproportionate or unrelated to that goal.

dimensions.detail: The name/description (agent session ops) match the provided materials: a context-usage script, hook patterns for checkpoint/rollback and token budgets, stale-session daemon patterns, and rate-limit detection for tmux panes. No unrelated credentials, binaries, or external endpoints are requested.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md and reference docs instruct the agent to read transcripts under sessions/, inspect tmux panes, send keys to tmux (with guard checks), create git checkpoints (git add -A + git stash create), and run or schedule daemons/cron. These actions are within the stated scope but are potentially impactful (sending Enter into a tmux pane or auto-applying stash can be destructive). The docs include explicit safety checks and warnings, which reduces but does not eliminate operational risk.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No install spec (instruction-only) and only one small bash script plus tests. Nothing is downloaded or written during install, so there is low install-time risk.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: No environment variables, credentials, or config paths are required. The skill reads standard project/session paths (sessions/<session-id>/ and transcript JSONL) that are reasonable for the described behaviors.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The patterns propose writing per-session files (heartbeat, checkpoint, trackers) and optionally running a daemon/cron. The skill does not request 'always: true' or system-wide privilege escalation, but it does assume write access to sessions/ and ability to run background checks; users should verify that file locations and permissions are acceptable.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill is internally consistent with its stated purpose, but several of its runtime actions are operationally risky. Before installing or enabling: 1) Review scripts (context-usage.sh, hooks) and understand where 'sessions/<session-id>/' lives in your environment; 2) Run the scripts in a safe/test workspace first — tmux send-keys and automatic git stash/apply can trigger destructive changes if mis-targeted; 3) Ensure the daemon/cron is run with least privilege and that session state paths are backed up or isolated; 4) If you don't want automatic interaction with tmux panes, disable or modify the rate-limit recovery component; 5) Consider code review / policy approval if this will run on production hosts. If you want, I can point out the exact lines to change to make actions safer (e.g., stricter pane matching, dry-run mode, or requiring manual confirmation).
